say: A JOIN lines up rows from two tables wherever the key values match. An INNER JOIN keeps only the matches. Joining delivered orders to customers gives 8 rows, each now with a name and city.
A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the first table, even with no match. The missing columns come back as NULL. That is how you find who is missing, like Funmi, a customer who has never received an order.
She starts from customers, so nobody is lost, and puts status equals delivered inside the ON part of the join, not in WHERE.

say: The gap is 82,000. After the join there are 11 rows, not 8, because three orders have two product lines each, so each is counted twice. This is called fan-out.
The quick test: compare COUNT star with COUNT DISTINCT order ID. If the first grows and the second does not, rows are repeating.

say: Five checks catch most silent errors. Does the row count make sense? Do totals reconcile? Is there fan-out? Are NULLs handled on purpose, for example with COALESCE to turn a missing value into 0? And did you spot-check two rows?

panel.heading: Before you share a number
items: Row count makes sense
Totals reconcile
No join fan-out
NULLs handled on purpose
Two rows spot-checked

say: To remember. Check counts and totals as soon as data is loaded. Use INNER JOIN for what was sold and LEFT JOIN for who is missing. Watch for fan-out. And never share a number you have not reconciled.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Check row counts and totals after loading
INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps everyone
Right-table filters for a LEFT JOIN go in ON
Fan-out inflates sums; test with COUNT DISTINCT
Never share a number you have not reconciled
